topics.name: Introduction to Language Models
topics.description: Language models are AI systems that learn to predict or generate text based on patterns learned from data. They form the backbone of many natural language processing applications by modeling the probability of word sequences to produce coherent, contextually relevant text.
topics.learning_objectives: Learn what a language model is and why such models are used in natural language processing. Understand the basic principle of how language models predict text based on context. Become familiar with examples of tasks that rely on language models (e.g., text generation, autocomplete). See how language modeling has evolved from simple statistical methods (like n-grams) to advanced neural network approaches. Appreciate the importance of language models as a foundation for modern NLP and AI applications. What are some real-world applications of language models in today’s technology (such as in virtual assistants or translation services)?

topics.name: Neural Networks and Transformer Architecture
topics.description: This topic explores the evolution of neural network approaches for sequence modeling, from recurrent neural networks (RNNs) to the Transformer architecture. It covers how Transformers, with their self-attention mechanism, overcame the limitations of RNNs and became the standard foundation for state-of-the-art language models.
prerequisites: None (basic understanding of machine learning is helpful but not required)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn how neural networks can be used to model language data and sequences. Understand the limitations of early recurrent neural networks (RNNs) in capturing long-range dependencies in text. Learn how the Transformer architecture functions, especially the role of the self-attention mechanism in processing sequences. Understand why Transformers revolutionized NLP and are now the dominant architecture for LMs, thanks to their ability to capture long-range context and train efficiently on large datasets. What architecture is predominantly used in state-of-the-art language models today, and what key mechanism makes it so effective?

topics.name: Pre-training and Large Language Models (LLMs)
topics.description: Pre-training is the process of training a language model on a massive corpus of text to learn general language patterns. This topic explains how large language models (LLMs) are built through this process, highlighting the importance of scale (in data and model size) in achieving advanced language understanding and versatile capabilities.
prerequisites: Familiarity with the concept of language models and neural network architectures (from previous topics)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn what “pre-training” means in the context of language models and why training on large unannotated text corpora is beneficial. Understand how large-scale pre-training enables models to learn grammar, facts, and general language patterns without explicit labels. What are some prominent examples of large language models (like GPT-3 or BERT), and how do their size and training data scale influence their capabilities? Understand the concept of emergent abilities: how very large models sometimes display new capabilities (such as few-shot learning) that smaller models do not. Recognize the difference between a pre-trained base model and a fine-tuned model, and why extensively pre-trained LLMs are often referred to as “foundation models” in AI.

topics.name: Fine-Tuning and Transfer Learning in NLP
topics.description: This topic covers how pre-trained language models are adapted to specific tasks or domains through fine-tuning. It explains the concept of transfer learning in NLP, where the knowledge from a general pre-trained model is leveraged to quickly achieve high performance on a downstream task by further training the model on task-specific data.
prerequisites: Knowledge of pre-trained language models and basic model training concepts (from previous topics)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn what fine-tuning means in the context of NLP and how it adapts a pre-trained model to perform a specific task or fit a new domain. Understand why fine-tuning is an effective form of transfer learning, leveraging the general language knowledge learned during pre-training to quickly achieve high performance on a target task. See examples of fine-tuning in practice, such as tuning a general language model for sentiment analysis or question-answering, and how this improves performance compared to training a model from scratch. What are the typical steps involved in fine-tuning a pre-trained language model on a new task? Understand the issue of catastrophic forgetting (how a model can lose earlier knowledge when fine-tuned on new data) and learn strategies to mitigate it (like using lower learning rates or regularization methods). Be aware of advanced fine-tuning techniques (such as adapter modules or parameter-efficient tuning) that allow updating a model with fewer parameters or less data. Recognize that fine-tuning has been the standard method for model adaptation, which newer approaches like self-adapting models seek to automate and improve upon.

topics.name: Continual Learning and Model Adaptation
topics.description: This topic introduces continual (lifelong) learning, where a model learns new tasks or information over time without forgetting previous knowledge. It examines the challenges in updating a model with new data (such as catastrophic forgetting of old knowledge) and why achieving continuous adaptation is difficult, highlighting the need for approaches like self-adapting models that aim for ongoing learning.
prerequisites: Understanding of model training and fine-tuning processes (Topics 3-4)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn what continual (lifelong) learning means for AI models and why it is important for systems that operate in changing environments or require ongoing adaptation. What is catastrophic forgetting, and why does it occur when a model is trained sequentially on new tasks or data? Discover methods proposed to enable continual learning, such as rehearsal (replaying old data), regularization techniques (like penalizing changes to important weights), and dynamic architecture approaches (adding new neurons or modules for new tasks). Understand the stability-plasticity dilemma: the balance between retaining past knowledge (stability) and learning new information (plasticity) that continual learning algorithms must achieve. See examples of scenarios where continual learning is desired — for instance, a language model that needs to keep up with new world events or a personal assistant that learns user preferences over time. Appreciate how the goals of continual learning tie into self-adapting models: both aim to let models update their knowledge over time, with self-adapting LMs being a specific approach to achieve continuous learning autonomously.

topics.name: Meta-Learning and Few-Shot Adaptation
topics.description: This topic covers meta-learning, or “learning to learn,” which trains models to adapt quickly to new tasks with minimal data. It discusses algorithms like MAML (Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning) that optimise a model’s parameters for adaptability, enabling few-shot learning. This approach to rapid adaptation complements the idea of self-adapting models by focusing on preparing models during training to be flexible when facing new tasks.
prerequisites: Familiarity with basic training and optimization concepts
understanding of fine-tuning and tasks (from previous topics)
topics.learning_objectives: What does it mean for a model to “learn how to learn”, and how do meta-learning approaches accomplish this goal? Understand the basic idea behind Model-Agnostic Meta-Learning (MAML) and similar algorithms, where a model is trained over many tasks such that it can adapt to a new task with only a few training steps. Recognize how meta-learning differs from standard training: rather than optimizing performance on a single task, it optimizes the model’s ability to quickly learn new tasks. See examples of few-shot learning enabled by meta-learning (for example, a model that can learn to categorize new types of data or perform a new language task using only a handful of examples). Understand how meta-learning contributes to model adaptability, complementing the concept of self-adaptation by preparing models that can quickly fine-tune themselves on new tasks. Note that even large language models not explicitly meta-trained often show few-shot learning abilities (they can adapt to new tasks via prompt examples), which hints at implicit meta-learning effects from broad training.

topics.name: Knowledge Editing in Language Models
topics.description: This topic explores techniques for updating a language model’s knowledge after it has been trained, without retraining from scratch. It covers “model editing” methods that allow specific facts or behaviors in a model to be changed or corrected (for example, fixing an outdated fact), while minimizing changes to the rest of the model’s outputs. This is related to self-adapting LMs, as both deal with updating model knowledge post-training, although knowledge editing is typically guided externally rather than by the model itself.
prerequisites: Understanding of model training and the relationship between model parameters and stored knowledge (Topics 3-4)
topics.learning_objectives: What are some reasons we might need to update or edit a language model’s knowledge after it has finished training? Understand the straightforward approach to model editing: fine-tuning the model on a small new dataset (for example, a corrected fact) and why this naive method can lead to unintended side effects (like altering other unrelated outputs). Learn about specialized model editing techniques that target specific knowledge in the model (for instance, methods that identify which part of the network to change for a given fact, such as the ROME algorithm) to minimize impact on other capabilities. See concrete examples of knowledge editing, such as correcting a model that gives a wrong answer to a factual question or updating it with a recent event, and understand how success is evaluated (the model changes on that fact but remains accurate elsewhere). Understand how model editing relates to model adaptation: both aim to adjust a model post-training, but typical editing is guided externally by a human or algorithm, whereas a self-adapting model would ideally handle such updates on its own. Be aware of the limitations and challenges of model editing techniques, such as difficulty scaling to many edits or ensuring the change doesn’t subtly affect other knowledge.

topics.name: Reinforcement Learning for Language Models
topics.description: This topic describes how reinforcement learning (RL) can be applied to train language models in scenarios where feedback is given as a reward rather than explicit correct answers. It highlights RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback) as an example, where models like ChatGPT are refined using human-preference signals, and provides context for how RL is utilized to train models to self-improve (as in self-adapting LMs).
prerequisites: Basic understanding of machine learning training and evaluation (prior topics)
no specialized RL knowledge required (fundamentals will be introduced)
topics.learning_objectives: Learn what reinforcement learning is and how it differs from supervised learning (using a reward signal for feedback instead of direct correct-output labels). Understand how a language model can be integrated into an RL framework: treating the model’s text outputs as actions and providing a reward based on the quality or correctness of those outputs. Learn about Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) as an example, where human preferences or a learned reward model guide a language model to produce more desirable responses (such as helpful or safe answers). See why RL can be useful for fine-tuning language models on complex objectives – for instance, optimizing for user satisfaction or task success when a simple labeled dataset is not available. Understand how RL fits into training a self-adapting model: the model is trained (via RL) to generate self-edits that yield better performance, using improvement on a task as the reward signal. What challenges arise when applying reinforcement learning to train language models (for example, issues with credit assignment in long text outputs and ensuring stable training)?

topics.name: Self-Adapting Language Models (SEAL) – Overview and Motivation
topics.description: Introduces the idea of self-adapting language models, where a model (such as in the SEAL framework) can update its own parameters in response to new inputs or challenges. It discusses the motivation for this approach – addressing the limitation that traditional LLMs are static after training – and gives a high-level overview of how a model can generate its own fine-tuning data and instructions to improve itself iteratively.
prerequisites: Familiarity with fine-tuning
continual learning
and reinforcement learning concepts (from previous topics)
topics.learning_objectives: What is a Self-Adapting Language Model, and how does this concept address the limitations of traditional static LLMs? Understand the motivation behind self-adapting models: recognizing that conventional LLMs cannot update themselves with new information or tasks once training is finished. Learn that the Self-Adapting LLMs (SEAL) framework was introduced by researchers as a way to give an LLM the ability to refine its own weights, effectively allowing the model to continue learning post-deployment. Understand at a high level how a self-adapting model operates: instead of relying on external retraining, the model generates its own training data and instructions (self-edits) to improve on a given input or task. Appreciate the significance of this approach: it allows the model to iteratively improve or acquire new skills on the fly, moving toward an AI that can continuously learn. Be prepared to explore the details of how a model can implement this self-adaptation in the following topics.

topics.name: Self-Adaptation Mechanism: Self-Edits and Weight Updates
topics.description: Delves into how a self-adapting language model actually performs an update on itself, expanding on the concept introduced in the previous topic. It explains the notion of “self-edits” – the model’s own generated instructions and data for fine-tuning – and how applying these self-edits via gradient updates changes the model’s weights, resulting in a lasting improvement to its performance.
prerequisites: Background in how model training updates weights (fine-tuning concepts) and the self-adaptation approach introduced earlier
topics.learning_objectives: What is a “self-edit” in the context of a self-adapting language model, and what information might it include? Learn the types of information a model can generate in these self-edits (for example, rephrased input data with correct outputs to form a training example, suggestions for optimization hyperparameters like learning rate or number of steps, or instructions to use external tools for gathering more data). Understand how the self-edit is executed: the model’s suggested update is taken and applied via a small fine-tuning step on the model itself, meaning the model’s weights are adjusted according to its own instructions. Recognize that these weight changes are persistent – after a self-edit and update, the model permanently incorporates the new information or skill, unlike just temporarily changing via context or memory. Draw an analogy to human learning: the model identifies an area for improvement and then “studies” that area by generating practice data or notes for itself, resulting in a lasting update to its knowledge. Understand that this mechanism effectively automates what would normally be an external fine-tuning process, enabling the model to handle it internally.

topics.name: Training Self-Adapting Models (Reinforcement Learning Loop)
topics.description: Describes how a self-adapting model is trained to generate useful self-edits, building on the mechanism from Topic 10. It details the reinforcement learning loop used in training: the model is rewarded when its self-generated updates lead to improved performance, thereby learning over many trials how to better adapt itself.
prerequisites: Familiarity with reinforcement learning and the self-edit mechanism (previous topics)
topics.learning_objectives: How can we train a model to generate effective self-edits, and what approach ensures that the model’s self-generated updates actually improve its performance? Understand the overall training strategy for a self-adapting model: first giving the model some supervised examples or guidance for generating self-edits, and then using reinforcement learning to refine this ability based on actual performance gains. Learn how a reinforcement learning loop is set up for this purpose: the model is tested on a new input, it produces a self-edit and updates itself, and then the updated model is evaluated on the task to determine a reward (improvement or not). Understand that the model receives positive reinforcement when its self-edit leads to better results on the task (and perhaps negative or no reinforcement if there’s no improvement), teaching it over many iterations which kinds of self-edits are beneficial. Recognize that this is an outer-loop training process, on top of the model’s regular training: the model is learning not just the task, but how to better train itself for the task. Appreciate the complexity and cost of this approach: each training iteration involves performing actual weight updates and evaluations, which makes training a self-adapting model resource-intensive and technically involved.

topics.name: Results and Case Studies of Self-Adaptation
topics.description: Reviews the key experimental findings from self-adapting language model research. It shows how these models performed on various tasks after self-adaptation, highlighting significant improvements (e.g., a model solving tasks it initially failed after updating itself) and discusses what these results imply about the potential of models that learn autonomously.
prerequisites: Understanding of the self-adaptation approach and its training (Topics 9–11)
topics.learning_objectives: Review the types of tasks and benchmarks on which self-adapting language models have been tested and evaluated. Learn how self-adaptation impacted performance on those tasks: note cases where a baseline model initially struggled or failed at a task but, after self-training, was able to succeed or achieve significantly higher accuracy. Recognize specific standout results from the SEAL approach, such as the dramatic improvement on the ARC-AGI challenge tasks (solving roughly 72% of those tasks after self-adaptation, up from 0% before any self-training). Discuss how efficiency played a role in these experiments (for example, understanding roughly how many self-generated training iterations or examples were needed for substantial improvement on a task). Learn about any limitations seen in the results – for instance, were there tasks where self-adaptation did not help much, or did the model sometimes produce ineffective updates – and what that means for the approach’s generality. What do these experimental results indicate about a model’s capacity to learn and improve autonomously?

topics.name: Self-Adaptation vs Other Adaptation Methods
topics.description: Places self-adapting language models in context by comparing this approach to other methods of model adaptation. It contrasts self-adaptation with traditional fine-tuning (human-guided updates), meta-learning (preparing models to adapt quickly), retrieval-based methods (using external knowledge without changing model weights), and parameter-efficient tuning, discussing the advantages and trade-offs of each approach in achieving model adaptability.
prerequisites: Understanding of self-adaptation (Topics 9–11) and familiarity with fine-tuning
meta-learning
etc. (earlier topics)
topics.learning_objectives: Compare the self-adapting model approach with standard fine-tuning: understand how self-adaptation automates and internalizes the adaptation process that is normally done by human engineers offline. Contrast self-adaptation with meta-learning: meta-learning trains a model that can quickly adapt when given new data by humans, whereas self-adaptation has the model actually generate that data and perform the adaptation itself in real time. How does using external knowledge retrieval (like searching a database or the internet for information) differ from having a model update its own parameters to incorporate new information? Examine parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods (such as adding adapter layers or prompt tuning) as an alternative way to quickly adapt models, and consider if such techniques might be integrated with self-adaptation for efficiency. Understand the unique strengths of self-adaptation (permanent improvement, reduced need for human intervention) versus its trade-offs (complexity and cost), in comparison to other adaptation methods. Appreciate the broader landscape of model adaptation strategies, seeing where self-adapting LMs fit among these approaches and how each can be suitable for different scenarios.

topics.name: Challenges and Limitations of Self-Adapting Language Models
topics.description: Discusses the current limitations and challenges faced by self-adapting language models. It covers issues such as the possibility of forgetting previous knowledge when learning new information, the heavy computational cost of performing self-updates, the difficulty of ensuring the model’s self-generated data is correct and safe, and broader reliability and alignment concerns when an AI is given autonomy to modify itself, in light of previous discussions.
prerequisites: Understanding of the self-adaptation mechanism and awareness of continuous learning concepts (Topics 9–12)
topics.learning_objectives: Identify the risk of catastrophic forgetting or model drift: if a model focuses on new training data, it might degrade in performance on older tasks or knowledge. Understand the high computational demands of self-adaptation: generating training data and fine-tuning on the fly can be slow and resource-intensive, which is a barrier to practical use with large-scale models. Discuss the quality control challenge: since the model creates its own training edits, there is a risk it could incorporate incorrect information or reinforce mistakes if its self-generated data is flawed. Examine safety and alignment concerns: an autonomous self-changing model could potentially learn undesired behaviors or go off track if its reward signals or constraints are not well-defined. Recognize the difficulty in monitoring and debugging: when a model changes itself, it becomes harder for developers to understand what modifications were made and why, complicating maintenance. What factors make self-adapting models an active research area rather than a widely deployed technology today?

topics.name: Future Directions and Applications of Self-Adapting Language Models
topics.description: Looks ahead at how self-adapting language models might evolve and be applied. It discusses potential improvements (making updates more efficient and safe), integration with other techniques (like external memory or guided feedback), and real-world applications — for example, AI assistants that continuously learn from users or models that keep themselves up-to-date with new information — and how these developments tie into the broader goal of AI that can learn autonomously.
prerequisites: Understanding of the capabilities and limitations of current self-adapting LMs (Topics 12–14)
topics.learning_objectives: Explore possible improvements to self-adapting models, such as making the weight update process more efficient (using smaller or modular updates) and adding safeguards to prevent forgetting and instability. Consider ways to combine self-adaptation with other techniques, for example using external memory or knowledge bases alongside self-updates, or incorporating human feedback to guide a model’s self-learning process. Discuss potential real-world applications of self-learning models: for instance, personal AI assistants that learn continually from their user’s interactions, or systems that automatically update their knowledge base as new information becomes available. Understand how advances in self-adapting LMs align with the broader goal of AI that can learn autonomously over its lifetime, reducing the need for human retraining intervention. Recognize the open research questions and challenges that remain, such as ensuring the safety of self-modifying AI and improving the reliability of autonomous learning. What might future AI systems be capable of if they can safely and effectively continue learning and adapting on their own after deployment?
